Based on the lecture slides, here's an explanation of the **MR (Marginal Revenue) curve** in this TNC market context.

## How the MR Curve is Constructed

The lecture uses a clever **analogy** to map the TNC problem onto a standard monopoly framework:

| TNC Market | Standard Monopoly Analogy |
|---|---|
| Driver wage \(w\) | Profit per unit \(\pi\) |
| Driver cost \(c\) | Marginal cost |
| Number of drivers \(\lambda\) | Quantity \(q\) |

The platform sets the driver wage \(w\) to maximize profit. The **MR curve** in the \(\pi\)-\(q\) diagram represents the **marginal revenue** generated by adding one more driver (or equivalently, one more unit of "quantity" \(q\)).

## Why the MR Curve is Downward Sloping

Since the TNC platform is a **monopolist** in the ride-sharing market, it faces a downward-sloping **demand curve** (DC) — as the platform serves more passengers (higher \(q\)), it must lower the fare to attract additional riders. This means each additional unit of service generates **less additional revenue**, which is why **MR lies below the demand curve** and slopes downward.

## Role of the MR Curve in Profit Maximization

The profit-maximizing point for the monopoly TNC platform occurs where:

$$MR = MC$$

That is, the platform keeps hiring more drivers until the **marginal revenue** from the last driver equals the **marginal cost** of employing that driver. The MR curve intersects the Marginal Cost (MC) curve at:

- \(w^*\) — the optimal driver wage (without regulation)
- \(q^*\) — the optimal number of drivers/quantity

## How Minimum Wage Regulation Affects the MR Curve

The minimum wage regulation (slides 10–13) doesn't shift the **MR curve itself** — rather, it shifts the **Supply Curve (SC)** and **Marginal Cost (MC)** curves upward (since the platform must pay a higher minimum wage). This changes the intersection point with MR, leading to three regimes:

1. **Minimum wage < \(w^*\)**: No effect — the optimal point \(q^*\) remains unchanged
2. **\(w^*\) < minimum wage < \(w_1\)** (where \(w_1\) is the wage at SC-MR intersection): More drivers hired, higher wages, more passengers served
3. **Minimum wage > \(w_1\)**: Fewer drivers hired, reduced service

This counterintuitive result — where a minimum wage can **increase** employment — is unique to the two-sided market structure of TNCs, where drivers and passengers are complements on the platform.

Slide 9 (page 9) introduces the **graphical framework** for analyzing the TNC minimum wage. Here's what it sets up:

## The Core Analogy

The lecture maps the TNC market onto a standard monopoly producer model by renaming variables:

| TNC Concept | Monopoly Analogy |
|---|---|
| Driver wage \(w\) | Profit per unit \(\pi\) |
| Driver cost \(c\) | Marginal cost |
| Number of drivers \(\lambda\) | Quantity \(q\) |

## What the Platform Does

The TNC platform is modeled as a **monopolist** that sets:
- The **driver wage** \(w\) (how much to pay drivers)
- The **number of drivers** \(\lambda\) (how many to hire)

## The Three Curves on the Graph

1. **Supply Curve (SC)** — shows the relationship between the equilibrium driver wage \(w\) and the number of drivers \(\lambda\). As more drivers join, wages adjust based on supply/demand matching between drivers and passengers.

2. **Cost Curve** — the platform's total cost of hiring drivers, i.e., \(\pi = \text{revenue} - \text{cost}\).

3. **Marginal Cost (MC)** — the additional cost to the platform of hiring **one more driver**.

4. **Marginal Revenue (MR)** — the additional profit the platform earns from adding **one more driver**. This is derived from the platform's revenue function.

## The Profit-Maximizing Point

The optimal \(w^*\) and \(q^*\) are found at the intersection **MR = MC**, which is the standard profit-maximization condition for a monopoly.

This slide is the **baseline** — no minimum wage yet. The slides that follow (10–13) then introduce the minimum wage regulation and show how it distorts this picture by shifting the supply curve and MC curve.

Great question. The "jump" on page 10 is the key insight of this slide. Let me break it down.

## Why the Supply Curve "Jumps"

Before minimum wage regulation, the supply curve \(SC\) is the standard upward-sloping relationship between driver wage \(w\) and customer arrival rate \(\lambda\). The platform is free to choose any \(w\) along this curve.

Once a minimum wage \(w_{min}\) is imposed, the supply curve gets **truncated**. The platform can no longer offer wages below \(w_{min}\). So the new supply curve under regulation becomes:

$$SC_{\text{new}}(w, \lambda) = \max(w_{min}, \text{original } SC(w, \lambda))$$

This means the supply curve effectively **jumps up** — it no longer starts at the low end of wages. Below \(w_{min}\), the original supply curve is simply cut off.

## Why This Matters for Marginal Cost

Since the **MC curve is derived from the cost function** (which depends on the supply relationship), the jump in the supply curve propagates to the MC curve. The MC under regulation **jumps upward** at the point where the minimum wage floor intersects the original equilibrium.

## The Intuition

Think of it this way: before regulation, if the platform wanted to serve fewer customers (lower \(\lambda\)), it could simply lower the driver wage \(w\) to reduce supply. After the minimum wage, this lever is **gone** — the wage can't go below \(w_{min}\), so the platform's marginal cost of reducing service is now higher. The platform is "stuck" paying \(w_{min}\) even when it would prefer to pay less.

This is what creates the three distinct regimes you'll see on pages 11–13 — the jump in MC shifts the \(MR = MC\) intersection in different ways depending on how high \(w_{min}\) is relative to \(w^*\) and \(w_1\).

## Total cost as an area

The total cost at any point on the supply curve is:

$$\text{Total Cost} = \int_0^N \omega(N') \, dN'$$

Geometrically, this is the **area under the supply curve** — which is the same as the total "compensation" paid to all drivers up to rate \(N\).

## With vs. without regulation

| | Without regulation | With regulation |
|---|---|---|
| Supply curve | Smooth, passes through \((\lambda^*, w^*)\) | Jumped up by minimum wage floor |
| Wage at \(N_0\) | Lower \(\omega(N_0)\) | Higher \(\omega(N_0) = w_{min}\) |
| Total cost at \(N_0\) | Smaller area under SC | Larger area under SC |

The minimum wage **raises the effective cost per driver**, so at any given \(N\), the platform pays more in total. The jump you asked about is exactly the difference between the original wage and \(w_{min}\) — and that gap becomes the extra cost burden per driver unit.

## The Driver Distribution \(F_d(\omega)\) and Total Cost

From the slide, the supply side is built from the **driver distribution** \(F_d(\omega)\) — this tells you how many drivers \(N\) are willing to work at wage \(\omega\).

## Total Cost at \(N_0\), With and Without Regulation

**Without regulation:**
The platform chooses wage \(\omega\) freely. At driver rate \(N_0\), the wage is determined by the inverse supply curve:
$$\omega = F_d^{-1}(N_0)$$

Total cost:
$$\text{TC}_{\text{no reg}} = \omega(N_0) \cdot N_0 = F_d^{-1}(N_0) \cdot N_0$$

**With minimum wage regulation \(w_{min}\):**
The platform can no longer pay below the floor. The inverse supply curve becomes:
$$\omega_{\text{new}} = \max(w_{min}, \omega)$$

This means:
- If \(w_{min} < \omega(N_0)\): no change — the floor doesn't bind
- If \(w_{min} > \omega(N_0)\): the wage is forced up to \(w_{min}\)

Total cost:
$$\text{TC}_{\text{reg}} = \max(w_{min}, \omega(N_0)) \cdot N_0$$

## The "Jump" in Total Cost

When the minimum wage **binds** (i.e., \(w_{min} > \omega(N_0)\)), the total cost at any given \(N\) jumps upward by:
$$\Delta \text{TC} = (w_{min} - \omega(N_0)) \cdot N_0$$

This is the extra compensation the platform must pay for every driver, simply because the wage floor prevents it from paying the market-clearing rate. The supply curve in the diagram "jumps" because below \(w_{min}\), the original \(F_d(\omega)\) relationship no longer applies — the curve becomes a flat line at \(w_{min}\).
Let me also connect this to the two regimes from page 8, which gives concrete intuition for when the jump matters.

Based on the slide text, the cost curve is defined as \(\pi = \text{revenue} - \text{cost}\), so the total cost is the wage bill paid to drivers.

## At \(N_0\) (a given driver rate), from driver distribution \(F_d(\omega)\):

**Without regulation:**
$$\text{TC}_{\text{no reg}} = \omega(N_0) \cdot N_0$$

Since \(N = F_d(\omega)\), the wage at \(N_0\) is \(\omega = F_d^{-1}(N_0)\). The cost is simply the area of the rectangle under the original supply curve at that point.

**With minimum wage regulation \(w_{min}\):**
$$\text{TC}_{\text{reg}} = w_{min} \cdot N_0$$

If the minimum wage binds, \(w_{min} > \omega(N_0)\), so:
$$\text{TC}_{\text{reg}} > \text{TC}_{\text{no reg}}$$

## The Difference (The "Jump")

$$\Delta\text{TC} = (w_{min} - \omega(N_0)) \cdot N_0$$

This extra cost comes from the platform being forced to pay \(w_{min}\) instead of the market-clearing \(\omega(N_0)\). Every driver at rate \(N_0\) now costs the platform more.

This is why the **supply curve "jumps"** in the diagram — the platform can no longer achieve lower cost positions that were previously available by lowering wages. The minimum wage floor creates a **horizontal cutoff** in the supply curve at \(w = w_{min}\), and the MC curve derived from it jumps up correspondingly.

This is the root cause of the three-regime behavior on pages 11–13: the minimum wage doesn't just raise wages, it reshapes the entire cost structure of the platform.

<user_query>
does government earn the same when tax is imposed on consumer & producer
</user_query>

Yes — and this lecture covers exactly this principle on pages 14–18 with the **congestion charge** example.

## Tax Incidence Equivalence

In a standard competitive market, a tax imposed on **buyers** and a tax imposed on **sellers** lead to the **same**:

- Equilibrium quantity
- Final price paid by buyers
- Price received by sellers
- **Total tax revenue for the government**
- Deadweight loss

This is because the market doesn't care who physically hands the tax money to the government — it only responds to the **price gap** between what buyers pay and what sellers receive.

## The Key Mechanism

| Scenario | Effect on price |
|---|---|
| Tax on buyers | Buyers demand less → demand curve shifts left → equilibrium price drops for sellers |
| Tax on sellers | Sellers supply less → supply curve shifts up → buyers pay higher price |

Both mechanisms produce the **same wedge** between buyer price and seller price. The final allocation of the tax burden (who pays more) depends on **relative elasticities**, not on whose name is on the tax form.

## In the Lecture: Congestion Charge

Pages 14–18 show this exact equivalence for TNCs:

- **Charge on passengers**: added to traveler cost as \(p_3\) → affects demand curve
- **Charge on drivers**: subtracted from driver wage → affects supply side
- **Charge on TNC platform**: absorbed by the platform → affects cost structure

The lecture explicitly states: *"All these congestion schemes are equivalent!"*

The proof on pages 19–20 shows algebraically that with a relabeling of prices (e.g., \(p_1' = p_1 + p_3\)), the three formulations are mathematically identical. The government collects the same total revenue regardless of who pays the congestion charge.

## In the TNC Lecture Specifically (Pages 14–18)

The congestion charge \(p_3\) per trip can be levied on three parties:

| Party | Effect | Revenue collected |
|---|---|---|
| **Passengers** | Added to traveler cost, shifts demand curve down | \( \lambda \cdot p_3 \) per unit time |
| **Drivers** | Subtracted from driver wage (each driver earns \(w - p_3\)) | \( \lambda \cdot p_3 \) per unit time |
| **Platform** | Absorbed as a cost, reduces platform profit | \( \lambda \cdot p_3 \) per unit time |

Since all three collect the **same total revenue** (\(\lambda \cdot p_3\)), and all three lead to the **same equilibrium \(\lambda\)** and the **same final prices**, the government is indifferent to who pays.

## The Intuition

The TNC platform is a **monopoly**, so it doesn't perfectly follow competitive market assumptions. But because the platform internalizes all three costs through its profit-maximization problem, the congestion charge gets factored into the optimal \(w\) and \(\lambda\) regardless of who writes the check. The charge creates the same price wedge between passengers and drivers in all three cases.

This is why cities often choose **which party to tax based on political feasibility**, not economic efficiency — the outcome for the government treasury is the same either way.

\subsection*{(2) Should the company also accept offer O2?}

Accepting O2 means committing to supply an \textbf{entire additional block of 100 MW} at the offer price $p_{\text{O2}}$. Unlike a continuous offer, block offers must be taken as a whole --- there is no partial acceptance. The company must therefore compare the \textbf{total cost} of producing this 100 MW block against the \textbf{total revenue} it would earn.

\bigskip
\noindent\textbf{Step 1: Current dispatch under O1 only}

From part (1), the optimal dispatch under O1 is:
\[
p_A^* = 100\ \text{MW}, \qquad p_B^* = 300\ \text{MW}, \qquad q^* = 400\ \text{MW}.
\]

\bigskip
\noindent\textbf{Step 2: Dispatch if O2 is also accepted}

If O2 (100 MW) is accepted, the company must also dispatch its next-available generation. The next-cheapest available generation after $p_A = 100$ MW is \textbf{unit A's second block} ($p_A = 100$ to $200$ MW), because:
\[
MC_A(200) = 1.7 + 0.08(200) = 17.70\ \text{\$/MWh}
\quad < \quad
MC_B(400) = 1.8 + 0.06(400) = 25.80\ \text{\$/MWh}.
\]

So the expanded dispatch is:
\[
p_A^{**} = 200\ \text{MW}, \qquad p_B^{**} = 300\ \text{MW}, \qquad q^{**} = 500\ \text{MW}.
\]

\bigskip
\noindent\textbf{Step 3: Cost of the additional 100 MW block}

The extra cost of dispatching the second 100 MW from unit A is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta C &= c_A(200) - c_A(100) \\
         &= \bigl[20 + 1.7(200) + 0.04(200)^2\bigr]
          - \bigl[20 + 1.7(100) + 0.04(100)^2\bigr] \\
         &= [20 + 340 + 1600] - [20 + 170 + 400] \\
         &= 1960 - 590 = 1370 .
\end{aligned}
\]

The \textbf{average cost} of this block is:
\[
\overline{MC}_{\text{block}} = \frac{\Delta C}{100}
= \frac{1370}{100} = 13.70\ \text{\$/MWh}.
\]

Note: this is not equal to $MC_A(200) = 17.70$ because the marginal cost rises linearly over the block.

\bigskip
\noindent\textbf{Step 4: Decision rule}

Accept O2 if and only if the offer price covers the total cost of the block:
\[
p_{\text{O2}} \times 100 \geq \Delta C = 1370
\quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad
p_{\text{O2}} \geq 13.70\ \text{\$/MWh}.
\]

Equivalently, accept O2 if $p_{\text{O2}} \geq \overline{MC}_{\text{block}}$; reject otherwise.

\bigskip
\noindent\textbf{Conclusion:}

Accept O2 if $p_{\text{O2}} \geq 13.70$~\$/MWh. If $p_{\text{O2}} < 13.70$, the revenue from the additional 100 MW falls short of its total production cost, and accepting O2 would reduce the company's profit. The key distinction from part (1) is that O2 is a \textbf{block offer} --- the company must evaluate the \textbf{total} (not marginal) cost of the entire 100 MW block against the total revenue.

\subsection*{(2) Should the company also accept offer O2?}

Accepting O2 commits the company to supply an additional quantity $q_2$ at a lower (or the same) offer price. The key question is whether this additional dispatch is \textbf{profitable}, i.e., whether the marginal cost of the extra generation is below the offer price.

If the offer price of O2 is $p_{\text{O2}}$, the company should accept O2 if and only if:

\[
\text{MC of the next cheapest MW} \leq p_{\text{O2}} .
\]

After accepting O1, the generation stack is already:
\[
B\text{ (first 300 MW)} \longrightarrow A\text{ (100 MW)}.
\]

The next cheapest MW comes from \textbf{unit A's second block} ($p_A = 100\text{--}200$ MW) or \textbf{unit B's second block} ($p_B = 300\text{--}400$ MW), whichever is cheaper at the margin. Compare $MC_A(200)$ and $MC_B(400)$ with $p_{\text{O2}}$:

\[
\begin{aligned}
MC_A(200) &= 1.7 + 0.08(200) = 17.70\ \text{\$/MWh}, \\
MC_B(400) &= 1.8 + 0.06(400) = 25.80\ \text{\$/MWh}.
\end{aligned}
\]

\textbf{Rule:} Accept O2 if $p_{\text{O2}} \geq \min\{MC_A(200),\; MC_B(400)\} = 17.70$.

If $p_{\text{O2}} \geq 17.70$, dispatch the next-cheapest block; if $p_{\text{O2}} < 17.70$, reject O2 (dispatching any remaining unit would lose money).

\textbf{Intuition:} The generating company should only accept an offer if the marginal cost of supplying the extra electricity does not exceed the price offered. The profit-maximizing dispatch always follows the \textbf{merit order} --- generators with the lowest marginal cost are dispatched first. Once all generators with $MC \leq p_{\text{MCP}}$ are fully dispatched, no further offers should be accepted.

\textbf{Conclusion:} Accept offer O2 only if $p_{\text{O2}} \geq 17.70$~\$/MWh. Otherwise, the marginal cost of additional generation exceeds the offer price, and accepting O2 would reduce the company's profit.
